newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Faction to offer Bhutto brother's widow leadership.
newsitem.headline: Faction to offer Bhutto brother's widow leadership.

text.p: Supporters of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's slain brother decided on Sunday to offer the leadership of their breakaway political faction to his Lebanese widow, sources in the group said.

The decision was made by the central coordination committee of Murtaza Bhutto's faction of the ruling Pakistan People's Party (PPP), which has been opposing Benazir Bhutto's government, the sources said.
There was no immediate word whether Ghinwa Bhutto, a former teacher who speaks English and French besides her native Arabic, would accept the offer.
The Shaheed Bhutto faction also demanded that a Supreme Court judge be appointed to investigate the killing of Murtaza and seven of his colleagues by police in Karachi on Friday.
The PPP government of Sindh province has already appointed a provincial high court judge to look into the killing, which has shaken the 43-year-old prime minister and rocked her government.

Earlier on Sunday, demonstrators clashed with police outside Murtaza's house, preventing President Farooq Leghari from making a condolence call. Eyewitnesses said the demonstrators chased police away as Leghari's motorcade approached the area in Larkana in Sindh province.
They said about 250 supporters of Murtaza blocked the road with burning tyres and chanted slogans accusing Benazir's husband Asif Ali Zardari of conspiring in the killing.
The demonstrators attacked police with sticks and stones. Police retaliated in kind, but there was no gunfire.
Murtaza's supporters also set fire to a police van and a motorcycle and stoned private vehicles in Lahore, capital of the central province of Punjab, eyewitnesses there said.

Ghinwa urged supporters to stay calm until a government inquiry had completed its work. "Even today people were raising slogans and I have asked them, let us curse the killers but let us not take names now," she told reporters.
Murtaza, 42, was shot and killed with six of his followers in a clash with police in Karachi on Friday night. Another of his supporters died of his wounds on Saturday.
A spokesman for Murtaza's PPP-Shaheed Bhutto group said the party had no confidence in the high court judge appointed to head the inquiry, Ali Mohammed Baloch.

He accused police of shooting dead one of the survivors while in detention on Sunday. He said the man, identified only as Asif, had been in the back of Murtaza's vehicle, but had escaped injury during the shootout.
The spokesman said Pakistani security forces had detained 3,000 faction members in the past few days. Karachi police confirmed only six arrests.

Surviving members of the powerful but divided Bhutto political dynasty came together at the family's ancestral home in Larkana to pay their last respects to Murtaza, who was estranged from his older sister for much of his turbulent life.
Nusrat Bhutto, accompanied by Benazir and another daughter, Sanam, laid red roses on Murtaza's grave on Sunday.

Nusrat later issued a statement, carried by the official news agency APP, saying that Murtaza's death was part of a conspiracy against the Bhutto family and denying reports that she had implicated Benazir and her husband.

"The vicious, malicious and the unkindest remarks attributed to me are only designed to create confusion in the people's mind with a view to diverting attention from the real culprits whom the independent commission will identify," she said.
Nusrat's husband, prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, was executed in 1979 and another son, Shahnawaz, died, possibly poisoned, in France in 1985.
The PPP-Shaheed Bhutto faction, which has called for 10 days of mourning and a three-day strike, accused Zardari on Sunday of engineering Murtaza's death.
A statement issued by Zafar Arif, a member of the central committee of Murtaza's faction, said Zardari had held secret talks with "criminal elements" in the security forces last week.
No comment was immediately available from Zardari, who is also investment minister in his wife's government.
Police say Murtaza's guards fired first in the shootout, but opposition politicians disputed their account.
The already depressed Karachi stock market, which reopened on Sunday after the Friday-Saturday weekend, slumped 1.61 percent in reaction to Murtaza's killing, dealers said.
They said Murtaza's death had fuelled political uncertainty and the market would suffer as long as doubts over the future of Bhutto's nearly three-year-old government persisted.
